what_this_is: Per-million-token LIST prices, fetched from OpenRouter's public model catalogue, used ONLY to compute a preflight upper bound on what one cycle can cost so the loop can refuse before it spends.
this_is_the_router_s_testimony: These are what OpenRouter's API reported its list prices to be at 2026-08-07T09:18:03Z. That is testimony (D-18), exactly like the served-model string and the provider name it reports. It is not a statement of what was billed, it excludes router surcharges and cache pricing, and prices change without notice. Refresh with tools/fetch_rates.py --write.
verified_note: Fetched from the provider's own API rather than typed by hand, which is stronger than the placeholder table it replaced and is still not a human confirming a bill.
what_a_preflight_bound_cannot_do: It cannot bind the provider. Only a provider-side spending cap does that.
It cannot account for router surcharges, cache pricing, or reasoning tokens billed separately.
It bounds the WORST case: every sample emitting max_tokens. Actual spend is recorded from each response's usage block and reconciled into the ledger.

LOCAL.note: Served on the custodian's own hardware. Zero marginal API cost; electricity and wear are real and not modelled here.

daily_ceiling_note: SOP §4 requires a hard spend ceiling per day, with the run refusing rather than truncating. Committed and actual spend accumulate in record/cycles/spend-ledger.json on the accepted branch; a cycle whose worst case would cross this ceiling refuses before its first call.
a_model_with_no_entry_here_is_refused: The loop will not solicit a model it cannot price. A missing rate is the condition under which an unbounded spend happens, so it is a refusal rather than a default.

web_search_usd_per_request._note: Per-request search pricing, from OpenRouter's web-search documentation. 'native' is deliberately absent: its price passes through the serving provider and is not published in the model catalogue, so a cycle using it could not be bounded. An engine with no rate is refused, exactly as a model with no rate is.

daily_ceiling_history.raised_by: the custodian, explicitly, for one experiment
daily_ceiling_history.why: Round 11 is the first round in which parties can FETCH the record rather than search for it. An agentic sample re-sends the whole conversation on every turn with another page appended, so its worst case is triangular in the number of turns: $73.34 against $8.01 for the same question without the capability. $25 refused it, which was the control working -- the bound is only that large because the budget was corrected the same day to price agentic turns instead of one completion.
daily_ceiling_history.what_this_does_not_change: The bound still over-states by construction: it assumes every sample emits max_tokens on every turn and fills its fetch budget. Across nine recorded rounds actual spend has been 0.18-0.24 of worst case, so a $73 bound has historically meant roughly $15 spent. The ceiling is raised to let the preflight approve the BOUND, not because that much is expected.
daily_ceiling_history.expected_to_be_lowered: Yes. This is an allowance for a specific experiment, not a new normal. If fetch rounds become routine the ceiling should be set from their observed actuals rather than left at an experiment's headroom.
